title: What to Feed Squirrels and Chipmunks, and What to Plant for Natural Food | Quiet Backyard Living
description: QBL wildlife field notes, natural-food and habitat ideas, careful feeding context and the real Chippy story.

copy.figcaption_1: Actual QBL backyard visitors. A photograph of feeding is not a dietary recommendation.
copy.span_2: The backyard regulars / A practical field notebook
copy.p_1: What to feed squirrels and chipmunks—and what to plant for natural food.
copy.p_2: What they eat, what we’ve watched, and why a place to live matters as much as a place to stop for a snack.
copy.figcaption_2: An unnamed chipmunk; not every photograph identifies Chippy.
copy.p_3: Acorns, hickory and walnuts, beechnuts, hazelnuts, seeds, berries, mushrooms, buds and shoots are among their natural foods.
copy.p_4: Seeds, nuts, berries, grains, mushrooms, fallen fruit and occasional insects all appear in a varied diet. What is available varies by place and season.
copy.p_5: These are examples of food in a varied natural diet—not a complete menu or feeding ration.
copy.p_6: At our feeding spots, the regulars have gone for seeds, corn and nuts. That is part of our backyard story. It does not prove a balanced diet, a safe portion or a good approach for every yard.
copy.p_7: Wildlife agencies caution that feeding mammals can change behavior, concentrate animals and spread disease. Check local wildlife guidance and favor habitat over creating a dependence on handouts.
copy.a_8: Read the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service feeding guidance.
copy.summary_1: What about peanuts, corn and fruit?
copy.p_8: Plain nuts and seeds, corn and small fruit pieces belong to our backyard feeding notes. That does not establish a balanced ration or make raw peanuts a universally safe choice. Get species-specific guidance rather than using a snack list as a complete feeding plan.
copy.summary_2: What should stay out of the feeding area?
copy.p_9: Keep salty or flavored snacks, candy, bread, chips, moldy nuts and spoiled leftovers out. Skipping junk food still does not establish that supplemental feeding is appropriate for your situation.
copy.summary_3: What about an injured or orphaned animal?
copy.p_10: Contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator rather than trying to feed or treat the animal yourself. See the linked wildlife-agency guidance.
copy.span_10: A place to live / The longer view
copy.p_11: Consider serviceberry, elderberry, mulberry, wild plum, chokecherry, crabapple, raspberries, blackberries or blueberries. Choose species that suit your region and site; the list is not a native-plant certification.
copy.p_12: Oak, hickory, black walnut, beech and hazelnut are possibilities to explore. Shrubs, wood edges and log piles can provide shelter too. Think mature size and your actual yard before planting.
copy.p_13: Food, water and nearby cover are connected. Manage any shared wildlife resource with local guidance and regular attention; this is not a feeder-hygiene protocol.
copy.figcaption_3: Our woodpile and feeding area, part of the real backyard setting.
copy.figcaption_4: Chippy, from the cabin journal—not an illustration or stock animal.
copy.p_14: The snack service became part of the cabin rhythm. Meet Chippy in the journal, follow the spring return, and see the old lumber that turned into a playground.
